subtopic: PROCEDURE IN RAISING QUESTIONS OF PRIVILEGE
PROCEDURE IN RAISING QUESTIONS OF PRIVILEGE
speechtext:
May I be permitted to make a statement at this time? Apparently my remarks on Monday have been interpreted by some members as changing the practice with respect to routine proceedings generally. I did not intend them to have that effect. I made my statement because I felt that last session I had allowed a practice to develop which permitted a member to rise at the opening of the house on a so-called question of privilege and to discuss certain matters which had taken place outside the house. That was a departure from our rules, and I did not think it was in the interests of parliament to allow it to continue. As Beauchesne states: "A question of privilege ought rarely to come up in parliament." He further states:
Wilful disobedience to orders and rules of parliament in the exercise of its constitutional functions. insults and obstructions during debate, are breaches of the privileges of the house.
These and other breaches of privilege, when they occur, should be brought to the attention of the house, and should be taken into consideration immediately and followed by the appropriate motion.
I do not need to remind hon. members that it is not a question of privilege whether a member should or should not have made a speech outside the house, or whether it would have been preferable to make it in the house. If the speech was made in wilful disobedience of the orders and rules of parliament, or contained libels on members, it would of course be a question of privilege which should be raised in the house. Otherwise the matter should be brought to the attention of the house by a question to the member or to the ministry when the orders of the day are called.
May I ask hon. members not to rise on questions of privilege unless they are satisfied that they are legitimate and not a so-called question of privilege.
My statement on Monday should not be interpreted in such a way as to prevent ministers, when motions are called, from
making important announcements of public policy. There is no positive rule to that effect, but it is a practice which has been sanctioned by usage both in the United Kingdom and in Canada. It has been my custom to allow the leader of the opposition to ask questions with respect to such statements. It is my intention to continue that practice. Of course no debate may take place at that time.
My anxiety is that I shall not, by any ruling I make, improperly curtail the rights and privileges of any hon. member, and I am confident that I shall have the continued co-operation of hon. members in my effort to carry out my duties in this manner.

speechtext: Is there any money of the government of Newfoundland on deposit with the federal government which can be used by the Newfoundland government for development purposes?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: NEWFOUNDLAND FUNDS ON DEPOSIT WITH FEDERAL GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Paragraph 2 of article 24 of the terms of union of Newfoundland with Canada reads as follows:
(2) Newfoundland will retain its financial surplus subject to the following conditions:
(a)	one-third of the surplus shall be set aside during the first eight years from the date of union, on deposit with the government of Canada, to be withdrawn by the government of the province of Newfoundland only for expenditures on current account to facilitate the maintenance and improvement of Newfoundland public services, and any portion of this one-third of the surplus remaining unspent at the end of the eight-year period shall become available to the province of Newfoundland without the foregoing restriction;
(b)	the remaining two-thirds of the surplus shall be available to the government of the province of Newfoundland for the development of resources and for the establishment or extension of public services within the province of Newfoundland; and
(c)	no part of the surplus shall be used to subsidize the production or sale of products of the province of Newfoundland' in unfair competition with similar products of other provinces of Canada, but nothing in this paragraph shall preclude the province of Newfoundland from assisting industry by developmental loans on reasonable conditions or by ordinary provincial administrative services.
In holding balances of the government of Newfoundland under this paragraph the government of Canada is acting in the relationship of banker to customer. Accordingly, it is not considered that the present balance should be made public by the government of Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. McCann (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my sole purpose in taking part in this debate at this time is to attempt to clear up some of the misunderstanding, ignorance and criticism with reference to the administrative side of the Department of National Revenue.
During the debate there has been considerable criticism-and I have no objection to criticism, but it has perhaps been more a matter of misunderstanding of the statutes and the regulations under which we have to work. I want to deal first with the customs and excise division of the Department of National Revenue.
During the debate the matter of the textile industry has entered largely into the discussion. Last night in this house the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees), as reported at page 337 of Hansard, said that he was glad that I was here and in the house, that he had some particular thing he wanted to discuss;

The Address-Mr. McCann and then he went on to say that as there were a number of textile mills in his own riding he would like to add his voice in asking the government to take steps to alleviate what amounted to a real depression in the textile industry. He said that the main cause of this depression is legalized dumping of American textiles.
That, Mr. Speaker, is a severe accusation to make. I do not think it can be verified by the facts that there has been any legalized dumping in this country at all. I am entirely in sympathy with the position of the textile manufacturers and workers in this country, because I am, like the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair), one of the representatives from the Ottawa valley. We depend upon the textile industry for employment, perhaps in the main or to a greater extent than upon any other industry that we have in the Ottawa valley. I believe there are some reasons which ought to be put before this house as to why the textile industry is in the position in which it finds itself today.
After the Korean outbreak, for instance, in June two years ago, it appeared that there might be a shortage of textiles. What was the result? The retailers in this country- the big departmental stores-stocked up as they had never done before. The manufacturing of textiles increased by over thirty per cent within an extremely short period. What do we find today? We find that those same retailers have on hand stocks that they have not yet disposed of. Statistics show that consumer buying and retail sales are up to normal. While I am not giving the figures in dollars and cents, those are facts that everybody knows. As a consequence of that position, the retailers are not in the market at the present time for increased supplies of textiles.
Another factor that has entered into the situation is importations of textiles into Canada, particularly from the United States. Let me say that the plight in which the textile industry finds itself in this country is not unique. It is the same position as that in which the textile manufacturers find themselves both in Great Britain and in the United States. As I said, there is another reason, and that reason is the almost parity of exchange that exists at the present time. Two years ago exchange was unfavourable to the buyer in Canada; at least the rate of exchange was ten per cent, and that was, of course, favourable to the United States seller. That condition has changed, and we are now on parity. That ten per cent difference in exchange was equivalent to a ten per cent additional tariff on the textile industry in Canada during the time that it was in effect.


The aocusation has been made that there has been a lot of dumping in this country. Let us see what is meant by dumping. Section 6 of the Customs Tariff Act provides for the imposition of an additional duty known as a special or dumping duty, in respect to importations of goods of a class or kind produced in Canada when, but only when, the import circumstances as defined by this section render the imported goods liable to this additional impost.
There appears to be a general assumption, particularly in periods of buyers' markets, that imported competitive goods are being "dumped" on the Canadian market if the import prices are below those of Canadian producers, and that a special and latent authority may be invoked to apply a dumping duty to those imports. Contrary to the popular impression that the application of this additional duty is by a latent and discretionary authority, the fact is that the imposition of this duty is entirely by statute. It is automatic and mandatory where liability as defined in the statute is incurred.
Generally, with some exceptions, section 35 of the Customs Act provides the valuation basis of imported goods for ordinary duty purposes, which is also the general valuation basis for determining liability to dumping duty. This value, in brief, is the fair market value of the goods when sold for home consumption in the country of export. The liability to dumping duty is incurred where the selling price to the importer in Canada is less than the fair market value in the country of export, as provided by this section. The extent to which the dumping duty may be imposed-and this is the application of it- is the difference between the value for duty purposes and the selling price to the importer in Canada, exclusive of all charges incurred on the goods after their shipment from the place whence shipment is made directly to Canada, but not exceeding fifty per cent ad valorem.
For a fuller understanding of the statutory basis of valuation of imported goods for ordinary and dumping purposes, and the circumstances rendering imported goods liable to dumping duty, the pertinent section of the Customs Act is section 35. Perhaps I might read it:
35. (1) Whenever any duty ad valorem is imposed on any goods imported into Canada, the value for duty shall be the fair market value of such or the like goods when sold for home consumption in the ordinary course of trade under fully competitive conditions, in like quantities and under comparable conditions of sale at the time when and place whence such goods were exported by the vendor abroad to the purchaser in Canada; or, except as otherwise provided in this act, the price at which the goods were sold by the vendor abroad to the purchaser in Canada, exclusive of

all charges thereon after their shipment from the place whence exported direct to Canada, whichever may be greater.
When valuation under that section is not ascertainable, valuation may be arrived at by another method under this statute. I read:
2.	When the fair market value of any goods is not ascertainable under subsection one, the value for duty of such goods shall be the nearest ascertainable equivalent of such value.
And when value is not ascertainable there is another alternative, such as in the case where like goods are not sold in the domestic market but are being produced exclusively for export. Valuation may be determined in that instance by two methods. The section continues:
3.	When neither the fair market value nor the equivalent of such value can be ascertained, the value for duty shall be the actual cost of production of similar goods at date of shipment to Canada, plus a reasonable addition for administration, selling cost and profit.
Or the value for duty shall not include the amount of any additional taxes, for instance, excise taxes and the like. It will be observed, Mr. Speaker, that valuation for duty purposes is predicated first on domestic market prices, or under subsection 3 on the cost of production in the country of export.
Section 6 of the Customs Tariff Act, which imposes dumping duty, reads in part as follows:
(1)	In the case of goods exported to Canada of a class or kind made or produced in Canada, if the export or actual selling price to an importer in Canada is less than the fair market value or the value for duty of the goods as determined under the provisions of the Customs Act, there shall, in addition to the duties otherwise established, be levied, collected and paid on such goods, on their importation into Canada, a special or dumping duty, equal to the difference between the said selling price of the goods for export and the said value for duty thereof . . .
That is, fifty per cent of the difference between the invoice price and the actual value of the goods. Then, subsection 2:
(2)	The special duty imposed by the preceding subsection shall in no case exceed fifty per cent ad valorem and the following goods shall be exempt from such duty:
(i) Goods of a class subject to duty under the Excise Act: *
(ii) Goods or classes of goods declared exempt by any order or regulation made by the governor in council.
(3)	Duties and taxes imposed in the country of export shall be disregarded in estimating the value for the purposes of said duty.
(4)	"Export price" or "selling price" in this section means the exporter's price for the goods, exclusive of all charges thereon after their shipment from the place whence exported direct to Canada.
Let me point out here that the provisions of section 35 of the Customs Act, which I have read, and section 6 of the Customs
The Address-Mr. McCann Tariff Act, are in conformity with the articles covering valuation for ordinary and dumping duty purposes in the general agreement on tariffs and trade, to which Canada, the United States, Great Britain, France, Czechoslovakia and other countries are all signatories.
The question as to the meaning of the word "fair" in the phrase "fair market value" which appears in section 35 (1) of the Customs Act, and section 6(1) of the Customs Tariff Act, has been considered. There is an understandable feeling that to be "fair" a "fair market value" should represent at least the cost of production of the goods with a reasonable addition for administrative expense, selling cost and profit. In the opinion of the Department of Justice, to whom this question was referred, a "fair market value" may bear no necessary relationship to production cost. A market value which is consistent, and not the result of temporary panic selling under extraordinary circumstances, may be a "fair market value" within the meaning of sections 35(1) and 6(1), although such value may be less than production cost. That is the opinion given by the Department of Justice.
It is a regular trade practice, both in the United States and in Canada, in respect to some seasonal goods, such as ladies' dresses, to reduce prices in the domestic market as the season advances, and they may be less than production cost. In the opinion of the Department of Justice, these low prices, when an ordinary trade practice and granted generally in the domestic market of the exporter, represent a "fair market value". A difficulty arises from the earlier season in the United States than in Canada due to the difference in climatic conditions. The reduced prices in the latter part of the season in the United States become generally effective in that market at a time and during the period in which the early season prices of Canadian produced goods would still obtain if not affected by competitive imports from United States sources.
There is special provision in section 43 of the Customs Act for the fixation of arbitrary values for duty purposes when authorized. Such values represent the value for ordinary duty purposes, and automatically involve liability to dumping duty. By this section, values may be established in respect to imported goods not entitled to entry under the British preferential tariff, where imports, while in accordance with the statutory values as provided by section 35, are under conditions such as to prejudicially or injuriously affect the interests of Canadian manufacturers or producers. Arbitrary values, however, are contrary to the valuation provisions of the

The Address-Mr. McCann general agreement on tariffs and trade, and may only be resorted to in respect to imports from signatory countries under the escape clause, article 19, of the agreement. This clause, however, also provides for withdrawal by signatory countries of a similar concession granted by them in respect to imports. So that if that method were used it would not be very long before there would be retaliatory methods, and perhaps in the long run we would lose.
I may say that in connection with the importation of goods both the importer and the exporter must take an affidavit, which is given to the department of customs and excise, that the goods are not sold below market value, and we require that in every case an invoice shall be signed by the vendor, and that it be produced covering the imported goods, bearing the following certificate of value:
That the said invoice also exhibits the fair market value of such or the like goods when sold for home consumption in the ordinary course of trade under fully competitive conditions, in like quantity and under comparable conditions of sale at the time and place of direct shipment to Canada, or the equivalent thereof, or where such fair market value is not determinable, the value shown is not less than the cost of production of similar goods at date of shipment to Canada, or the equivalent thereof, or where such fair market value is not determinable, the value shown is not less than the cost of production of similar goods at date of shipment to Canada plus a reasonable advance for administration, selling cost and profit, and that the said fair market value
(a)	is without any discount or deduction not shown and allowed and deducted on invoices covering sales for home consumption in the country of export in the usual and ordinary course of trade; and
(b)	is without any deduction on account of any subsidy or drawback of customs duty allowed by the government of any other country, or on account of any royalty actually payable thereon when sold for home consumption, but not payable when exported, or on account of the exportation thereof; or for any special consideration whatsoever-
Now, an affidavit almost similar to that is taken by the importer. It is in these words:
That the value for duty of the said goods as stated in this entry exhibits the fair market value of such or the like goods when sold for home consumption in the ordinary course of trade under fully competitive conditions, in like quantity and under comparable conditions of sale at the time and place of direct shipment to Canada, or the equivalent thereof; or if such fair market value is not determinable, the value shown in this entry is not less than the cost of production of similar goods at date of shipment to Canada, plus a reasonable advance for administration, selling cost and profit, and that the said fair market value (a) is without any discount or deduction not shown and allowed and deducted on invoices covering sales for home consumption in the country of export in the usual course of trade; and (b) is without any deduction on account of any subsidy

or drawback of customs duty allowed by the government of any other country, or on account of any royalty actually payable thereon, or payable thereon when sold for home consumption, but not payable when exported, or on account of the exportation thereof; or the amount of consideration or money value of any special arrangement between the exporter and the importer, or any persons interested therein, because of the exportation or intended exportation of such goods, or for any special consideration whatsoever; that if the value for duty of the said goods as stated in this entry is other than the value thereof as above specified such value for duty has, to the best of my knowledge and belief, been fixed and determined under the authority of the Customs Act at the value stated in said entry.
Now, we do collect dumping duties, where the law applies. Last year we collected $1,547,289. Those were special or dumping duties.

Yes, but I cannot give a break-down as to the particular articles against which these dumping duties were imposed. However, that is the figure with reference to the extra, special or dumping duties, as they are known.
I admit frankly that I do not know what the solution of the problem is. I do know, however, some of the alternatives. One of those alternatives would be to increase the tariff. Well, the general opinion among countries of the democratic world, as was shown at the Geneva meetings, has been that there should be a tendency toward freer trade. I believe we would be very unwise to take the position that we would have to give more protection to any industry in Canada at the present time.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: No one suggested that.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I do not say the hon. member suggested it; I am only setting out the alternatives. Another alternative would be the matter of arbitrary valuation, whereby officials of the department would say arbitrarily what shall be the value of goods coming to this country.
In connection with ascertaining values I would point out that we have people in the United States, and in other countries, including Great Britain-and we used to have more than we have now-who are continuously giving us information with respect to fair market values in those countries. We receive the information through the trade sources we have in every country, and through our diplomatic service in those countries. Therefore we cannot be accused of not making an attempt to find out what fair market values are, and to apply duties where applicable. We cannot be accused of failure

to do everything we can to guard our own industry, consistently with the laws of our country.
I believe I have taken all the time I should take in dealing with this particular matter. I should like now for a few moments to deal with the taxation division of the Department of National Revenue.
Speaking in the house a few days ago the. hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue), among what he chose to term the gripes he had-no, I believe he used the word "beefs"- said:
The next beef I have to deal with has to do with the taxation division, and particularly the taxation of farmers.
I do not know exactly the definition of the word "beef", but my own definition would be that it is a type of grievance about which a complainant has knowledge, but as to the accuracy of which he has not much confidence. However, last December when he was discussing this same matter the hon. member made the accusation that the administration of the Department of National Revenue has been playing politics, so far as the farmers are concerned. That accusation is entirely unfounded. I wish to refute it immediately; I do not think it does justice to the actual thoughts of the hon. member for Assiniboia.
As I said earlier, the hon. member took occasion to criticize the administration in connection with the taxation of farmers. As I said before, honest criticism is not resented, but when the hon. member gives his opinion that the administration is, to use his own words, "playing politics so far as farmers are concerned", the time has come for me to reply.
The first remark I have to make is to deny flatly this charge of political interference. In the seven or eight years I have been head of the department, I have prided myself that there was absolutely no political interference. My one aspiration was to do a complete and honest job, irrespective of politics. That, I submit, I have accomplished one hundred per -cent.
Each district office in the taxation division is charged with the responsibility of assessing and collecting the income tax arising within its area, and there is no understanding whatsoever, written or implied, that any class of taxpayer should be overlooked or in any way treated otherwise than as prescribed in the Income Tax Act. The taxation of farmers across Canada is absolutely free of any political bias. Anyone who has knowledge of the workings of our large departments of government will readily appreciate 55704-24
The Address-Mr. McCann this. The day-to-day administrative decisions must be made largely by or on the advice of officials who have no concern whatsoever with politics.
Judgment as to where to place the emphasis in collecting income taxes must almost invariably be exercised by these officials, because they alone have the required experience and knowledge. The officers who determine these matters in the taxation division are men in whom I have the utmost confidence-and I have been associated with them perhaps longer than any other minister who has been in the department over the years.
I believe that all hon. members who have had dealings with these officials will testify that this confidence is not misplaced. They are not infallible; they make mistakes, like the rest of us, but when they do they are honest mistakes. The government, as is its duty, keeps close watch on the administrative policies of the taxation division, but, I repeat, there has never been an instance to my knowledge in which these officials were instructed to discriminate either against or in favour of any class of taxpayer in any locality, for any reason. I can state positively that the same honest effort is being made to collect income taxes from farmers in the east as in the west. The fact that the amounts collected are smaller in some provinces than in others is due to circumstances other than any inclination either on the part of the government to play politics or on the part of the income tax officials to neglect their responsibilities.
Before going further, I should like to emphasize that the figures which have been quoted as the income tax paid by farmers represent only the taxes declared voluntarily. Substantial increases-in the aggregate for all classes of taxpayers they run to tens of millions of dollars each year-are obtained by the income tax assessors. Information regarding these increases is not compiled by the taxation division in a form which can be used to make detailed comparisons between the various types of taxpayers in different parts of Canada. Considering the fact that the annual income tax collections amount to thousands of millions, the increases obtained are not a large proportion of the total collections, and, for this reason, the published statistics are quite satisfactory for the purpose for which they are prepared. On the other hand, they do not properly reflect the administrative efficiency of the taxation division, and were never designed for this purpose.

The Address-Mr. McCann However it is not my purpose to quarrel with the various figures which have been presented, but rather to disagree emphatically with the conclusions which have been drawn from those figures. In the first place it must be appreciated that income tax is not calculated on the average income of a whole group in any locality but upon the actual income received by each individual taxpayer. No one can determine how many taxpayers of any type there are in any area, or how much tax they should pay as a group, except by ascertaining the net income of each individual in the group and applying the provisions of the Income Tax Act to the exact circumstances of each individual case.
Criticism based on averages can be very misleading. For example, by using authoritative average income and average exemption figures a case can be made that farmers in the east should pay no income tax at all and that farmers in the west should pay substantially more than they are now paying. I would not present such a proposition to the house because it is entirely ridiculous. I mention this observation merely to show how meaningless and misleading averages can become if they are used unwisely. Consequently I submit, if they are used, that the figures presented to the house on previous occasions properly prove only one fact, namely, that the aggregate of the income tax collections from farmers in the western provinces is substantially greater than that collected from the farmers in the eastern provinces.
I admit that immediately. This has been so for every year for which we have a record, going back as far as 1926. Even in the 1930's, with drought on the prairies and very low wheat prices, there was nevertheless more tax collected from prairie farmers than from all the rest of the farmers in Canada. It was not many years ago that certain segments of the public were criticizing the department because the taxes collected from farmers in the country as a whole were in their opinion too low and reflected partiality, or at least inefficiency, on the part of our administration. During the course of the past few years the affairs of the western farmers appear to have improved to the point where significant amounts of tax are now collected and accordingly the criticism has shifted to a comparison between the west and the east. The logical explanation would seem to be simply that farming in Quebec and the maritime provinces, with some exceptions, is not yet sufficiently prosperous to provide very much income tax revenue under the present levels of personal exemptions. Let me point out that even in the prairie provinces which most fMr McCann.]

people regard as predominantly agricultural -note this-fewer than one out of every five farmers are taxable and that the aggregate of taxes paid by persons other than farmers in the prairie provinces is more than five times that paid by farmers.
To use averages such as those set out on page 1541 of Hansard of December 3, 1951, in the speech of the hon. member for Assini-boia (Mr. Argue), to attempt to prove that a proportionately larger amount of the actual income tax due is being collected from western farmers than from eastern farmers, is erroneous. It may or may not be a fact that the taxation division is getting proportionately more of the tax actually payable from western farmers than from eastern farmers. I am not prepared to deny or to confirm this because I have not, nor has anyone else, sufficient information to prove the point one way or the other; but I do say very emphatically that these figures are of no real value when we are looking for an answer to this question.
Certain hon. members feel that we do not tax farmers in Quebec and Ontario with the same efficiency that we do out west. The fact is, however, that there are units of men specializing in the assessing of farmers' returns in the Montreal, Quebec and Sherbrooke offices just as there are in the prairie districts, and similar procedures are followed to find new taxpayers and to check the returns which are filed. The same holds true in Ontario. Let me cite some instances of what has been done.
During the past several years surveys have been made of the rural areas in all provinces of Canada, both in the east and in the west, to build up the tax rolls of farmers. These have generally involved the examination-I am disclosing some of the methods that we use-of municipal assessment records and the obtaining of information regarding specialized types such as tobacco and dairy farmers. For example, in the Montreal income tax district in 1946 such a survey was made which resulted in the issuance of 30,000 requests to farmers to provide information and the subsequent receipt of over 14,000 returns. The vast majority of these were determined to be non-taxable and the responsible officials did not consider at that time that large-scale investigation would prove effective in increasing the revenues. Similar surveys, but perhaps on a smaller scale, have been carried out on a more or less continuous basis in subsequent years in the Montreal and other income tax districts. The type of action taken has been varied between income tax districts in accordance

with the facts and circumstances, but it can be definitely stated that the same honest effort has been made to obtain income tax from the Quebec and Ontario farmers as from those in the prairie districts.
A staff of income tax assessors dealing exclusively with farmers has been maintained which is in relation to the expected revenues and the relative importance of farm activities from the income tax point of view in each locality. There are actually about eighty of these assessors in Ontario, which is more than in any other province, and this has been the situation for several years. The next largest staff of farm assessors is in Saskatchewan where there are about sixty. The staff of twenty odd in Quebec may seem small in comparison. Nevertheless a survey by departmental officials in 1950 of estimated staff requirements, which took account of all the available information regarding the possible revenue to be obtained from farmers and other relevant factors, did not recommend any substantial change or increase.
As in any department run on a businesslike basis, every effort is put forward to make the best possible use of the available manpower in our several income tax offices. Having regard to the potential tax dollars to be realized, the number of farm assessors in Ontario and Quebec is probably already high in relation to the number in western districts. The proportionately larger staffs are considered to be justified because the task of finding the comparatively few farmers who are actually taxable in an area such as Quebec is more difficult than in the west, and it is also more difficult to determine the actual income on which the tax should be based. These are the reasons. This is so because more of the business is done by cash in Quebec, the records maintained are usually inadequate, and the products sold are in great variety.
In the more prosperous farming areas in the west the number of products dealt in is generally smaller, the majority of sales are made in large amounts mainly at one season of the year, and records of many of these sales are readily available. Nevertheless a real effort has been made in all localities, and I assure you that this will continue. As indicated earlier, the rural areas are being continually surveyed in an effort to discover additional farmer-taxpayers. I can also state that very careful analyses of all internal and external statistics that bear on this subject are continually being carried out. If the results of further study indicate that the department would be justified in assigning additional personnel to examination of this class of return, you may be assured that the necessary steps will be taken.
The Address-Mr. McCann
Another instance may be cited of unfounded criticism based on general statistics. During the last session a member pointed out that there are many more farmers located in our Edmonton district than there are in the Calgary district but that the revenue from the farmers in the Calgary district was six times that obtained in Edmonton. The facts are that the taxing of farmers in both districts is carried out in exactly the same way and with equal efficiency but that the fewer farms in the Calgary district are larger and more prosperous, with the natural result that more revenue is obtained from the smaller number. These figures again illustrate the futility of attempting to reach conclusions from statistics alone regarding the amounts of tax which should be obtained from farmers in different areas where the circumstances are entirely different.
As I stated earlier, there is only one way to determine how many farmers should be paying income tax in any locality, and that is by definitely and accurately ascertaining the net taxable income of each individual farmer. On the other hand there are certain facts which were not taken into account in the figures presented to the house on the 3rd of December, 1951, which appear to explain a substantial part of the difference between income tax payments by farmers in the west and those in the east, particularly in the province of Quebec.
In the first place the occupied farm land and the average area per farm is substantially greater in the prairie provinces than in easterri Canada. For example, the province of Alberta alone has a greater area of occupied farm land than Quebec and Ontario combined. Furthermore the average size of farms in the prairie provinces is from two and one half to three and one half times as large as those in Ontario and points east. It is also a fact that the size of the farm family is so much larger in Quebec than for example in Saskatchewan that a farmer in Quebec will on the average have to earn almost $500 more each year before he will become subject to the same tax as a Saskatchewan farmer. To illustrate the significance of even this single factor it is pointed out that the aggregate taxes declared by Saskatchewan farmers in 1949 would have been reduced by about $1,500,000, if each of the 20,000 odd who made these declarations had been entitled to claim an exemption equivalent to that of the average Quebec farmer.
There are numerous other factors, such as the actual farm incomes, the expenses of operation, donation payments, the amount of supplementary income from investments and so on, medical expenses, the effect of special

The Address-Mr. Coldwell provisions in the law such as the averaging of income, which would have to be considered to get a proper and complete explanation for differences in income tax collections between different localities. It is virtually impossible to get together sufficient information to estimate the effect of each of these and the many other factors that go into the calculation of an income tax assessment. Sufficient has been said, however, to show the futility of jumping to conclusions on the basis of one or two factors only.
I have seen fit to put this explanation on record at this time, Mr. Speaker, with a view to clearing up some of the misunderstandings which I realize have existed with reference to both divisions of the Department of National Revenue.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Because I do not expect to be here most of tomorrow and Friday I am taking the opportunity this afternoon of participating in this debate because of a speech over the radio last evening by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson). I am glad indeed that he is in his seat this afternoon; otherwise perhaps I would have hesitated to say what I am going to say.
First I want to thank the minister for sending me a copy of the speech he delivered. I was surprised at its content. Last Thursday when I criticized the Lisbon conference in this house I said I had no doubt my remarks would be misrepresented and misconstrued, but I did not think the Secretary of State for External Affairs would stoop to the deliberate smears in which he indulged last evening.
It has become apparent on this continent that constructive criticism made necessary by the demands of military leaders of NATO is invariably criticized as communist propaganda. I do not have to defend myself against the charge of communism. I have been an outspoken opponent of it all my life; but the inference that what I said the other evening and what was said by the national council of the C.C.F. was the Kremlin line is something the minister himself must know to be untrue. I want to say that I approved of the statement of the national council. Let no one think I was pushed into a corner by any members of our organization in approving of the statements that were issued in regard to international affairs. When the meeting was called I asked our national secretary to include international affairs on the agenda. I introduced the subject. I first made the criticisms that were included in the national council's statement; and I am going to say this afternoon that in regard to NATO at least the criticisms that were made were

justified and can be documented. Last evening the minister did not attempt to document any of his criticisms of our position.
After saying last evening that there is no danger of aggression from Russia, but that the Russians charged that we were trying to build up our strength in NATO as an aggressive military alliance-and I have disagreed with that-he said:
It is sad to see that the C.C.F. seem to be moving towards this position. The statement issued on Wednesday last by their national council charged that, and I quote, "NATO policies seem to have fallen completely under the control of the military." They found proof for this strange assertion in the fact that at Lisbon we decided on a program of 50 divisions for western Europe by the end of 1952 and 90 to 100 divisions, including Germany, by the end of 1954. These decisions the C.C.F. council described as "irresponsible and disastrous." That is exactly how the Kremlin would describe them. The C.C.F. then urges Canada to oppose vigorously the armaments goals set at Lisbon which they claim represent increases in the military program.
In fact, these goals do not represent increases but decreases over those that were set a year ago and which the C.C.F. approved.
Last Thursday evening I drew attention to an editorial in the London Times, a conservative or independent paper, whichever you care to call it, with an international reputation. That newspaper criticized the Lisbon statements in these words:
It is difficult to understand either the meaning or the purpose of the communique published by the council of the North Atlantic treaty in Lisbon. This states in words which seem almost to have been chosen for their ambiguity-they have no other virtue-that the member nations will provide this year "approximately fifty divisions in appropriate conditions of combat readiness." Only the most ingenuous will suppose that General Eisenhower will in fact have fifty divisions ready and able to fight in Europe by the end of the year. The exact figures are rightly secret, but the present force is generally believed to be rather less than half that number. Since no German divisions will be raised this year, since contributions from Greece and Turkey are not included in this total, and since France has been allowed to reduce her contribution from fourteen to twelve, it is not easy to see how this figure can be substantially increased. Certainly Britain is not going to send more divisions to Europe this year, and it would be surprising indeed if the United States were to fill the gap. The explanation probably is that the phrase "in appropriate conditions of combat readiness" is meant to include not only divisions fully trained and equipped for war but other divisions half-trained and half-equipped, reserve divisions like our own territorial units, and yet other divisions which so far exist only on paper. No doubt it is necessary to plan for such an expansion, but it is less obvious why it should be announced in this airy fashion.
Then it goes on:
Presumably the announcement was meant to impress someone; but it will not impress the Russians, who know very well the true state of affairs and who have the sense to realize that any real plans for real divisions would be kept secret. Indeed this imaginative total, with the still more

imaginative promise of 85 to 100 divisions in two years' time, seems to contain the maximum amount of provocation with the minimum amount of deterrent effect.
"The maximum amount of provocation." If that is what has been done, is that not irresponsible? And if the result is as the London Times has stated, won't it be disastrous? I used those two words, then, "irresponsible and disastrous". That is what the London Times says, not only what I say or what the C.C.F. says.
Now, it goes on to say this:
Perhaps it was meant to impress the European nations themselves, who will thus feel that something is being done on the grand scale to justify their effort and expense. Unfortunately, it is more likely to have the directly opposite effect of creating a sense of false security, and of glossing over weaknesses and omissions in the existing arrangements for defence.
Would not that be disastrous? Is that not irresponsible, to mislead the European nations to that extent?
Even if it is meant only to impress the American congress-and the whole communique has a very American ring-it may fail in its object for there is likely to be a sharp reaction when the American people realize that the fifty promised divisions do not really mean fifty divisions and that much money and effort will still be needed if Europe is to be made safe.
If that is the result of this statement, is that not going to be disastrous to the defence of the free world? Is it not irresponsible to mislead our great neighbours to the south as well as other people, to the extent that the Lisbon statement has misled them? I quote again from the article:
Part of the trouble is no doubt caused by a mistaken attempt to combine military security with political propaganda. The Atlantic community, it is felt, should behave in an open, democratic way.
There is nothing open, and nothing democratic in the manner in which this program has been undertaken.
To be effective, however, military planning, as the Americans are well aware when dealing with such matters as atomic energy, requires a measure of secrecy. To escape from this dilemma the Atlantic council has apparently hit on the device of a kind of mock publicity which pretends to tell everything while revealing nothing and boasts of divisions in nice round numbers of fifty or one hundred without giving away any vital information. It is a bad device because it effectively hides both the real progress that has been made and the weakness that must be made good. It also suggests that the planners, who as recently as November were talking quite happily of forty divisions in 1952, and who are now asking for fifty instead and for eighty-five or one hundred in 1954, do not really know what they want or what they need. Such erratic reckoning bears no evident relation to the real and calculable danger which has to be faced in Europe.
This ends the Times editorial.
To underline this statement, let me quote from some authoritative papers, but more
12, 1952
The Address-Mr. Coldwell briefly this time. What about the London Economist, one of the outstanding papers of its type in the world. In the issue of March 8, which has just been received by airmail, there is an article headed "Phantom Divisions". I may say that the Times editorial was headed "The Phantom Army". The Economist says:
The Atlantic council which assembled in Lisbon rashly allowed itself to say that some fifty divisions "in appropriate conditions of combat readiness" would be provided to defend western Europe in 1952.
As was pointed out on all hands, if combat readiness means the same as "ready to fight immediately" then the statement must be quite untrue and therefore inexcusable.
Irresponsible and disastrous, those are our words. The London Spectator of February 29, 1952, had this to say:
To talk of "fifty divisions in appropriate conditions of combat readiness" as the target to be reached by the end of this year is the most outstanding ambiguity. There is no pretense that the force which General Eisenhower or his successor will have under his command onj the continent of Europe by the end of 1952 will be anywhere near this figure.
Deceptive, irresponsible and if believed disastrous. I could quote from other papers, but I have chosen to quote from conservative papers instead of from a paper such as another I hold in my hand, the New Statesman and Nation.
Let us look more closely at the minister's statement. He stated that the new goals of fifty divisions in 1952 does not represent increases but decreases over those which were set a year ago, and which we of the C.C.F. approved in this house. First of all, let me say that I have never heard any mention of the number of divisions in this house or any support requested for any number of divisions. The New York Times on November 25 referred to the military targets for NATO in the following words:
Originally General Eisenhower was aiming at sixty or more divisions by 1954. The western big three still hope this target can be met; but they agree the emphasis in the next year should be on getting somewhere between twenty-six and thirty divisions in battle readiness. Presently SHAPE has the rough equivalent of twenty divisions but many of these divisions are raw recruits.
James Reston, the well-known correspondent of the New York Times, wrote on December 5, 1951, that General Eisenhower has implied that a situation of strength will exist in western Europe only if the western allies manage to have about sixty fully equipped divisions by July 1954, and about thirty of these available in 1952. To confirm that, last November the New York Times published a chart. I cannot put that chart on the record, of course, but what does it show? It shows that in February, 1951, General Eisenhower had seven NATO divisions in Europe. Then,

The Address-Mr. Coldwell that is in November, he had twenty-two divisions. The goal at the end of 1952 was twenty-eight divisions, and the goal by the end of 1954 was sixty divisions. All of a sudden we are told that we are to have fifty divisions this year and one hundred in 1954. The minister says there has not been any increase in the last year in the number of divisions planned, not any increase but a decrease. Well, I always thought that ninety was more than sixty. I always thought that fifty was more than twenty-eight.
Of those divisions in Europe, the maximum the United States will have there at the end of 1954, according to this chart, would be six. The remainder would be raised in Europe. The minister says there has not been an increase, but a decrease. What did NATO say? It issued a bulletin at the close of the Lisbon conference on February 24 of this year. Let me read paragraphs two and three from an original release dealing with the numbers:
By its resolution on the TCC report, the north Atlantic council agreed on specific policies and plans for building NATO defensive strength during the present year. NATO nations agreed to provide approximately fifty divisions in appropriate conditions of combat readiness and 4,000 operational aircraft in western Europe, as well as strong naval forces. It further provided a definite program for taking measures this year necessary to increase the defensive power of NATO in following years. This defensive force does not include the contributions of Greece and Turkey.
There was general agreement that this increase in defensive power will constitute an important increased deterrent against aggression. While not covered specifically by the council action at Lisbon, it was recognized that allied strategic air power is already a powerful deterrent to aggression and in the event of attack would be a most valuable addition to the defence of western Europe.
I understand the minister was chairman of the conference. How on earth he could go on the air last night and tell the people of Canada that the Lisbon agreement did not provide for an increase but, on the contrary, for a decrease, in the face of the statement of the organization itself, I do not know.

The next thing I want to say is this. Apparently Dean Acheson did not have the view that the minister now says that he had. I have in my hand a verbatim copy-allegedly ait least-of Dean Acheson's radkntele-vision. address on February 29, when he returned from Lisbon, with regard to the matter we are now discussing. This is what he said, according to the New York Times of March 1:
The first thing we wanted to do at Lisbon was to reach agreement on a realistic plan for increasing NATO's military forces. The supreme command must be assured of the largest number of effective combat forces that can be developed this year, and we wanted to lay the groundwork for further increases . . .
Then he went on to say:
The estimates for 1952 were accepted as firm goals.

In the kind of world in which we live today, it is no good having goals unless you are going to reach them. The minister cannot get out of his difficulty in that way. The next thing was this. The minister says that what was done at Lisbon the C.C.F. members of this house-and other members too, of course-approved. What did we approve? At no time were any figures regarding NATO targets placed before this house. The estimates for Canada's contribution to NATO, the United Nations forces and for our own defence were placed before parliament on February 5 last year and were subsequently approved by the house, and we gave our approval to those estimates. I looked up the records last evening, carefully, after I had seen the minister's speech and I found that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) outlined the government's proposals. As reported in Hansard of February 5, 1951, at page 95, he said:
The role of Canada in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization has now been determined in consultation with the other eleven nations. Canada intends to do everything necessary to carry out that role. The program put forward here includes everything necessary to do that.
That is the program of last year. Shorn of its details, the program envisaged Canada's obligations over the next three years. Those obligations involved an expenditure of approximately $5 billion. The Minister of National Defence said this:
To carry through these plans during the next three years the strengths of the three forces should be increased to about 115,000 full-time active service personnel and about 33,000 civilians.
That is what we voted for. That is what the house voted for. He also outlined the gifts that we had decided to make in equipment to European countries, and he said this:
This is a program, a large one for a country of 14 million people still involved in developing its natural resources and also facing the task of maintaining essential services over an area of 31 million square miles.
He placed the expenditure involved at over $5 billion. For this we voted, and the national council statement, which the minister criticized last evening, stated in its very first sentence "that we continue to support the North Atlantic Treaty Organization".

speechtext: The McCarthy line.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
What a slander! That slander went out over the air and was scattered widespread over the country.
May I digress for a moment, Mr Speaker. When I was in church last Sunday morning, I happened to pick up the leaflet in my seat. It told the story of a woman who had an uneasy conscience. She went to her spiritual adviser, told him that she had repeated gossip
The Address-Mr. Coldwell about her neighbours, and her spiritual adviser said: "Go to the market and get a freshly killed chicken. Walk away with it, and as you walk away, pluck it. When you have taken all the feathers off, come back to me." She came back and she said: "I have done what you told me to do; I have done my penance." She was then told: "Now, go back again and pick up the feathers". She said: "I can't. They are scattered to the winds. They are gone beyond recall." That is exactly what has happened with the kind of smear and slander that was put out over the air in this country last night by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson). You cannot gather up the feathers. You cannot recall the slanders. They are there, and there are people who will repeat them and believe them because they want to believe them. So when we say in the very first words that we continue our support of NATO, I ask you, Mr. Speaker, this question: Does that appear that we are moving in the direction of the communist position? Obviously the minister's style last night was that of Senator McCarthy in the United States where already thousands of people are afraid to express an honest opinion because they may be characterized as subversive, communist, enemy of the state or what you will. The C.C.F. statement suggested that the armament goal set at Lisbon, for, as the London Times said, the military agreements, contain "the maximum amount of provocation with the minimum amount of deterrent effect." That is not my statement. That is the statement of the London Times, agreed to by the Economist and endorsed by the Spectator, and by other papers that have taken the trouble to go into this matter.
What did we urge? We urged what we have always urged from the beginning-and we supported this at the outset. We urged that a substantial proportion of the total sums involved in NATO goals should be diverted from crippling and excessive military preparedness to necessary rebuilding in Europe and elsewhere. I want to say to the minister and to the house that you cannot build defence when there is economic disease in Europe or anywhere else. We said that because we believe and believe honestly-and we are entitled to these opinions-that the policy outlined at Lisbon jeopardizes the peaceful and defensive objectives which brought the organization into being. Does that sound like a communist line?
Even before the Rome and Lisbon meetings, almost every responsible statesman in Europe had warned against overexpansion of military commitments. Mr. van Zeeland, when he was in this city of Ottawa in September of

The Address-Mr. Coldwell last year, here in this very chamber as chairman of the NATO meeting, spoke of a major menacing factor within the treaty organization. What factor did he say? The financial-economic pressures set up within member nations because of the armament program. This was echoed by the former chancellor of the exchequer of Great Britain, Mr. Hugh Gaitskell, by numerous statesmen in France where even today they have no government that can possibly remain in power more than a few hours. A significant statement was made by Mr. Churchill when he criticized Aneurin Bevan who, may I add, opposed the armament program in Britain last year. We supported Canada's program. But Mr. Churchill said that Mr. Bevan had been right for the wrong reasons. And last week, as I quoted last Thursday evening, Mr. Churchill said in the House of Commons that Britain could not fulfil the former three-year program in three years. She would need at least four. And yet, how many divisions are the United States to have in Europe by 1954? Six. Where are the others to come from? From Germany? Greece and Turkey of course are excluded under the Lisbon statement. Let me say this to the minister. Does he think that, when be used the word "disastrous" in his statement regarding our attitude on NATO and linking it with communism, it would not be disastrous if Germany was rearmed before she is integrated with the west? Would not that be disastrous? Should not integration come first? And yet the NATO people at Lisbon, were preparing to rearm Germany before any agreement regarding integration had been reached.
And should de Gaulle come to power in France, in view of the difficulties there, what then? And whenever the economic difficulties increase in France de Gaulle is that much nearer his objective of power. We all know that as far as the sterling area is concerned, that great group of nations comprising the United Kingdom and members of the British commonwealth-except Canada-and the Scandinavian countries were in the position where their economies were tottering last winter. The Netherlands is in a worse condition than some of the other western European countries.
From time to time the minister has spoken about the necessity for economic aid; but I cannot find where very much has yet been done regarding economic aid for the depressed peoples of the world. That is the only way in which we shall have a defence against communism.
In view of this, our strong words are warranted, and they were strong words in the statement and in what I said last Thursday


evening. I ask, were we not right in saying that the announcements made from Lisbon were, not in our opinion but in the opinion of these great newspapers that I have quoted as well, irresponsible, and may even become disastrous in the light of the economic situation that is developing in Europe?
I want to repeat what I said in effect the other evening. It is not we who are playing into the hands of the Kremlin, but those who are demanding more sacrifices from the overburdened, the harassed people of western Europe, who are all in danger of economic collapse, the collapse for which the Kremlin is waiting, because it believes that nation after nation may fall into its lap like ripe plums from an over-laden tree.
The minister stated that our statement was inaccurate in its facts and unfair and misleading in its conclusions. I think I have quoted sufficiently the relevant facts and conclusions, and I challenge the minister and anyone else to prove that they are inaccurate, unfair or misleading. Again I want to say that to endeavour to stifle honest, well documented criticism of any policy by smears, as in this instance, by gross inaccuracies as well, serves no useful purpose in this time of difficulty in which we live.
I have dealt only with these criticisms that the minister made in regard to the inaccuracy and the irresponsibility and the disaster the minister claimed was inherent in our statements. I could have gone into the matter of the vast expenditure proposed of $300 billion, and I shall probably do so when we are discussing NATO on a future occasion. I could have analysed that and shown how, if it is impossible for the European nations particularly to carry the burden today which, added up together in their budgets and including United States budget, amounts to about $212 billion, when you put another $100 billion on that you will see what will happen. United States congress is saying that they have to pare the budget this year. Are we prepared to vastly increase our expenditures? I would be prepared and my party would be prepared to support additional appropriations for economic aid so that the peoples of Europe and Asia could be weaned away from communist propaganda by the only manner in which they can be weaned away, namely, by improving their standard of living. That is all I have to say this afternoon, but, as the minister will understand, I deeply resent the slanders that went over the air last night from the mouth of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson).

Mr. Speaker, it is in no perfunctory sense that I extend to the mover (Mr. George) and the seconder (Mr. Gauthier, Lake St. John) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne my very sincere congratulations. And I should like as well to tender congratulations to the newest member of the house, the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Nickle), who, in his maiden speech in the house last Thursday night, made what I consider a very constructive and illuminating contribution to the knowledge of the house and to the quality of its debates.
This speech from the throne is likely to challenge competition with all others in the fact that it contains so little. It is the thinnest kind of throne speech one could well imagine for times like these. The great issues that should concern parliament and do concern the Canadian public today are not to be found within the scope of that speech. They lie outside it.
Those great issues today are the issues of overtaxation, inflation, the high cost of living and associated questions. We look in vain through this throne speech for any indication that the government is conscious of the need for taking prompt and effectual measures to cope with the difficulties created for the Canadian people by these policies of the governmen:.
Sir, the business of the house at this early stage of the session is, I think, deserving of comment. At the last session we had a committee to study the rules of the house. That committee laboured at least long and arduously and brought in a report at the end of the session recommending that the house should adopt permanently, by way of amendment of the rules, the hours of sitting which had been in vogue on an experimental basis during the fall session. It made other recommendations as well. Sir, I hope that the recommendations concerning the hours of sitting will not be overlooked at this session, and that the experiment which proved beneficial last year will be continued and made to operate under the rules of the house.
I urge again, as I have on other occasions, that the time of this house be conserved so far as possible by the use of committees of the house to undertake the detailed work of the session. There are two measures proposed in the speech from the throne this year, namely a revision of the Criminal Code and a revision of the Immigration Act, which it seems to me are matters eminently suitable for review in special or select committees of the house. I do urge again, as did my leader last Thursday, that every effort be made to facilitate the work of the house.

The Address-Mr. Fleming It can be done, with general approval on the part of all members, so as to avoid much of the overlapping that has existed in times past in the course of debate.
There is one aspect of the subject to which my leader referred in his speech last Thursday on which, for some reason or another, the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) made no comment. When the leader of the opposition urged that there should be no thought given to a repetition of any fall session in this year 1952, such as we had last year, no comment was made in reply. Why the Prime Minister did not see fit to give the kind of assurance that ought to be given on that subject, I shall continue to wonder. But I do wish to echo what the leader of the opposition said, that this parliament cannot expect to maintain the respect of the people of Canada and at the same time cotntemplate a fall session this year. The business outlined in the speech from the throne does not warrant it. If the business of the house is organized so as to be carried out effectively, there will be no occasion whatsoever for putting the taxpayers of this country to the expense of a second session of parliament this year.
There were one or two observations by the Prime Minister in his contribution to the debate on March 8 that, I think, fell on our ears with a measure of surprise. In replying to the argument of the leader of the opposition that a duty rests upon private members, regardless of party, as well as upon members of the opposition, to scrutinize what the government does or proposes in the house, the Prime Minister said., as reported at page 170 of Hansard:
I have no quarrel with him-
He was referring to the leader of the opposition.
-for his suggestion that it is also the duty of the opposition, and even of all members of parliament, freely to express their minds about the propriety or impropriety of the administrative acts that it is the duty and responsibility of the government, under the constitution, to have carried out in the name of the sovereign.
Fair words, Mr. Speaker-fair words, indeed! They sound almost like an invitation to government supporters in the house to speak and think independently. But, in case we were likely to be impressed unduly by fair words such as these, we had only to look across at the treasury benches and see there, at that very moment, sitting cheek by jowl with the Prime Minister, that member of the government who last year, in very contemptuous tones, said, in this house to members of the opposition, "If we wanted to get away with it, who would stop us?"

The Address-Mr. Fleming And we have had so many and such abundant proofs that the true attitude of the government toward the house is reflected, not in those fair words of the Prime Minister last Thursday, but in that studied and contemptuous attitude taken toward the house by the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) on that occasion-yes, and on many others, as well!
However, there is a note of warning here for private members who have hitherto given their political support to the government, because the Prime Minister on this occasion did not choose to accept on behalf of the government the full blame, for blame it is, for the way in which the plundering financial policies of this government have been working a hardship upon the taxpayers of this country.
On that occasion he sought to share the responsibility for this unhappy and calamitous result with the private members supporting him in the house. He indicated even that it is their responsibility. Well, we of the official opposition have been saying that for some time, that those Liberal members in the house who, by their acquiescence, their timidity and their silence have permitted the government to impose upon the people of Canada those heavy and extortionate levies, must share with the government that heavy responsibility before the bar of history.
I recently turned up a verse of Shelley written over a century ago, but which could well have been written in the lifetime of this parliament to describe the way in which some members of the house, by their acquiescent attitude, have permitted themselves to be subjugated by the government. This is the verse:
Power, like a desolating pestilence,
Pollutes whate'er it touches; and obedience, Bane of all genius, virtue, freedom, truth, Makes slaves of men, and, of the human frame, A mechanized automaton.
The time has come in this House of Commons for the government to address itself to some very serious issues, and to pay a 'little less attention to its present concern for filling positions and dispensing patronage. On that subject alone I think the house would be interested to know what some Liberals in Toronto had to say not long ago about the way in which the government has consistently overlooked -the claims of the fair sex to appointments. This is a report from the Globe and Mail of Monday, February 25, concerning a meeting of the Ontario Women's Liberal Association. It reads as follows:
A charge that the government has consistently failed to accord recognition to women active in the Liberal party in conferring honours and making appointments was made Saturday by Mrs. Angus 
Gordon, convener of the political educational committee of the Ontario Women's Liberal Association at a meeting of the executive here. Mrs. Gordon said this was in the main the reason the association has difficulty in directing younger women into its membership. "We have in the ranks of Liberal women across Canada many outstanding women both willing and able to fill appointments to national and international boards", she said. She called upon Liberal women "to stand together and demand recognition of the work they have done and no longer show a willingness to be hewers of wood and drawers of water in political work."
One can admire at least the independence and the outspoken comments that fell from the lips of that distinguished lady. Is it too late, Mr. Speaker, to hope that something of that type of independence of approach may yet be expected on the part of some private members of the house who give their political support to the government?

We heard the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) announce last Thursday that on April 8 he will introduce his budget. I do not make bold to suggest the kind of budget the Minister of Finance ought to introduce in the house on that occasion. The minister has shown many times that he is not interested in suggestions of that kind coming from the opposition. But I am going to have some observations to make on this important subject today, and I do so without being deterred in the least by the very touchy attitude displayed by the Minister of Finance of late in the face of criticisms that are being levelled against the results of his policies.
It would better behoove the Minister of Finance, instead of being so critical of those who have criticisms to make, to address his efforts to removing the causes of outraged feelings on the part of many Canadian taxpayers whose businesses he is busily smothering under his arbitrary impositions. There is a very good test of freedom of expression offered here today. It appears from the remarks that the Minister of Finance made last Friday that he is seeking to discredit those in this country, and they are legion in number, who are criticizing his policies. I do not think the house is likely to see for a long time any more convincing demonstration of irresponsibility on the part of a minister of the crown than that offered to us last Friday by the Minister of Finance when he read in the house a letter written by an individual undertaking to condemn a certain

corporation, and said at the same time that he took no responsibility for the contents of the letter. Apparently he had not made the slightest investigation to determine whether the contents of the letter were true or false. He put it on the record anyway, and gave the most widespread publicity to something for which he himself admitted he was not prepared to take any responsibility. To my way of thinking that is proof abundant of utter irresponsibility.
What kind of budget should Canada be given this year? It should be a budget that will give the Canadian people needed reduction of taxation, that will relieve them from discriminatory fiscal burdens, and will eliminate waste and extravagance. The Prime Minister apparently sought to discourage criticism in the house on this subject by attempting on March 6 to sound the death knell of the hopes of so many Canadians who are burdened so heavily by the government's taxation imposts. At page 173 of Hansard he is recorded as having said:
But so long as the world situation continues as it is. I cannot hold out any hope to the Canadian people of any substantial reduction in the scale of the rate of taxation in this country.
The people of this country are not going to be satisfied to be pushed aside with remarks of that kind. Those of us who do not allow ourselves to have short memories with regard to this government's attitudes will, of course, treat this as equivalent to an announcement that there will not be a general election this year, and in the light of what happened in this country and in the house in the spring of 1949 will also be equally confident that regardless of what may develop in the world situation between now and then we will be told in the house on the eve of the dissolution of parliament that the world situation has improved, that the buoyant revenues available so fill the coffers of the government that sweeping reductions in taxation are at last possible, and that those reductions in taxes will then-not now- be a good thing for Canada. That is a little prediction in which I am bold enough to indulge today.
