Let us not have any more talk from the government about the impossibility of making reductions in the burden of taxation. Only yesterday the chancellor of the exchequer in the parliament at Westminster, in a country that is faced with infinitely more serious problems than we are and with a far more difficult financial picture facing the chancellor of the exchequer than faces our Minister of Finance, found it possible to bring relief to the taxpayers of Great Britain in the form of substantial reductions in income tax. There is an example for the Minister of Finance.
On the subject of credit restrictions I wish to say that I do not think anybody ever deluded himself that if fiscal measures of that kind were applied they would not hurt somebody in some degree; but look at the way the government went about the application of fiscal measures of this kind! Without applying them at an earlier stage and doing it in a reasonable way they waited, and when they did decide to act they acted harshly, suddenly and in a very discriminatory way. The discrimination is shown by the way in which these credit restrictions have singled out certain industries as particular victims for these policies of the government, the motor car industry, the leather goods industry, the tobacco industry, the electrical goods industry. These measures have not been uniform in their application. They have been grossly and cruelly discriminatory. We were told at the time that these policies, which were going to have the effect of reducing

The Address-Mr. Fleming the demand for materials for civilian production, were going to be so beautifully dovetailed with the government's policies with respect to rearmament. But what have we seen? Dovetailing? They simply have not had any relation to one another, and these industries and their employees have suffered harsh and discriminatory treatment on the part of the government.
When the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair) suggested, as he did in this house two days ago in a flight into the realm of sheer fiction, that what is going on out in British Columbia, where certain retailers of electrical goods are offering people credit of $150 for a cup and saucer, is the result of legislation passed by this house last December in regard to resale price maintenance, how absurd it was! If he would get down and examine the facts, if he would use his talents in that way instead of making these windy speeches in the house, he would soon find out that what is being done out there as well as elsewhere in Canada is an attempt to meet these heavy and burdensome credit restrictions which the government has imposed. I hope the people of Canada will realize that they were not imposed by direct parliamentary enactment, but by order in council. Parliament has simply been informed after the fact.
In the meantime, following the same kind of government policies, we see unemployment mounting throughout the country, the direct and inevitable result of this floundering government policy. In my own city at the last report the registered unemployed totalled over 31,000, and the situation is relatively equally bad in many other urban municipalities. How this government can manifest such utter indifference to that situation I am sure will defy all comprehension! The answer given people who are going hungry today, and who are lining up at hostels, is "Oh, well, your problem is only seasonal. You are the victims of seasonal unemployment", as if to be told that is a substitute for food in their stomachs or decent beds at night.
Last week, commenting on this subject in this house, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) said they were receiving unemployment insurance. Well, by this time it should be fully understood by the minister, should it not, that unemployment insurance has been very slow in being paid. In Toronto the delays have been from two to five weeks in the processing of claims. I venture to say you will not find anywhere a better example of governmental incompetence than those delays which are imposing great hardship on people in this country who are entitled to better treatment. It is not their fault they are unemployed. He

gives twice who gives quickly; and those who are entitled to unemployment insurance should not be compelled to wait these long periods of time. It must be clearly understood also that the scale of unemployment insurance is not adequate for those who are breadwinners with larger families.
On that occasion I asked the minister about those unemployed who come into the cities in times like these. We used to call them transients, though that is not an accurate term. They come to the cities because they think there is work; they hear about so-called defence contracts, and naturally come to the industrial centres. I asked the minister what he was going to do about those people. With the most surprised and amazed look he turned to me and gave a reply to the effect that he was not prepared to make a statement on that matter at that time. That was last Thursday; we have not had the statement yet. In the meantime, because of the failure of the government's credit restrictions and taxation policies to mesh in with their policies of defence production, the government is simply throwing upon the municipalities the burden of meeting the needs of those unemployed; and that is not good enough. Apparently the government has no policy with respect to the employable unemployed. I say to you, sir, it is high time they had one, instead of leaving this burden to bear upon the already overburdened property owners in the municipalities.
Now I wish to make a comment on the subject of expenditure. Let it be clearly understood that this budget surplus of $721 million at the end of the ninth month of this fiscal year is not attributable to retrenchment or thrift on the part of the government. There has been no retrenchment; there has been no thrift on the part of the government. Even on non-defence expenditures the government has been spending on a bigger scale than ever before. You remember that dramatic moment last April while the minister was delivering his budget speech, when he came to announce that little $35 million reduction in estimated non-defence expenditures for this fiscal year as compared with last year. With almost a catch in his voice he turned around to thank his colleagues on the treasury benches for the way they had been sitting up at night working so hard to pare down expenditure, as though they had been digging their knives into these estimates until the blood ran. Well, it was a heroic moment. But what do we find? Far from that little reduction of $35 million in non-defence expenditures, which you will remember was less than one per cent of the total budget of $3,700 million, the minister has had to

announce figures showing that in the first nine months of this fiscal year non-defence expenditures were actually $37 million more than in the first nine months of the previous fiscal year. It is in view of such facts that the Canadian Chamber of Commerce recently said, in a brief submitted to the Minister of Finance:
The federal budget is now so large and the tax burden so onerous that higher taxes enter our costs of production more quickly than under less stringent circumstances and are reflected in higher prices. Thus at a high level of taxation the stabilizing influence of a balanced budget tends to weaken and become less effective. The chamber therefore feels that a searching examination of government expenditures in all departments should be made: economy in government is as essential to the economic health of the country as economy in business is to the health of business.
As between the so-called two old parties differences of approach as far apart as the poles have become crystal clear in connection with this question of taxation and its function in our economic and political system. You will find the theory of the government in the speech the other day by the Prime Minister, as you will find it in many other speeches from the government side. Referring to the fact that in the first nine months of this year each family in Canada paid in taxation $250 more than was required to meet the legitimate expenses of government, the Prime Minister said at page 172 of Hansard:
And if the amount of commodities had remained what it was and there had been $250 more purchasing power for every family of five-well, in my simple logic I would come to the conclusion that that would have added to the inflationary pressure instead of the fact of its having been withdrawn as purchasing power adding to the inflationary pressure.
There you have it. The theory of the government is that they are conferring a favour upon the people by relieving them of this burden of surplus purchasing power. They say they are doing a good thing for the people, that they are managing the economy, and therefore they soak the people and at the same time say it is a good thing for them.
The approach of the Progressive Conservative party to this question of taxation is poles apart from that sort of approach. We say that taxation should be designed to meet the legitimate expenses of government. As for debt reduction, we say it should be budgeted for, that we should plan to retire debt in a systematic way. But we say the people are best able to manage their own affairs; and we lack no evidence that the people of this country are much more economical in the management of their own funds than is the government in the management of the funds
The Address-Mr. Fleming of the people. Let me quote very briefly what was said by the Montreal Star of February 20 on this subject:
The traditional principle of public finance is that a government should carefully estimate its expenditures and then take from the taxpayers only what it needs to carry on for the next twelve months. The money is our money, not the government's money, and no government has the right to take a nickle more than it needs to provide the services which parliament has agreed are necessary.
We in the official opposition know, even if the government does not, how this heavy taxation is hurting the people.
The government is also busy explaining the subject of the budgetary surplus. The government is busy trying to make a virtue today out of a non-budgeted, adventitious surplus, although the government was not prepared a year ago to practise the same virtue, because the budget surplus estimated last year was a mere $30 million. There was no lip service given then by the hon. gentleman opposite to the virtues of a big budget surplus, and the public I am sure is not going to be overwhelmed by all the nonsense that is being talked today by the government about the value of this surplus when they did not think enough of the subject last year to aim for one. We see today that in nine months this budget surplus has amounted to $721 million. In other words, the Minister of Finance made an error to the tune of 2,300 per cent in his calculations of the surplus, and we are not through with the year yet. In the face of that fact the government is today cheekily trying to make a parade of the fruits of this gross and colossal blunder.
We of the Progressive Conservative party have an entirely different view of the budget surplus. We want to see careful, accurate budgeting. We demand an end of this loose guesswork on the part of the Minister of Finance. We want to see the budget balanced with some reasonable provision for a budgeted plan of debt reduction, but we do not want any of these adventitious surpluses to tempt the spending appetite of this government. In the midst of warnings from the treasury benches that the government surplus may be less by the end of the year, I simply add that apparently the government are already devising ways and means of relieving themselves of what may be an embarrassingly heavy surplus by planning more expenditures. That is what they did a year ago. At that time they saw that the budget surplus was going to amount to something like eighteen times what they had estimated. They got busy and found ways in the dying moments of the fiscal year to spend $150 million in order to get that surplus down to ten times what the minister had estimated.

The Address-Mr. Fleming
I ask, sir, where are the January figures? It is the practice to issue those figures of revenue receipts and expenditures in the Canada Gazette on or about the 20th of the month following. We have not seen those figures that were due around February 20. We are now into March, so where are the figures for the tenth month of the fiscal year?
How did this budget surplus come about? It came about, first, by grossly, unforgivably and misleadingly inaccurate budgeting; second, by punishing rates of taxation; third, by utterly unnecessary increases in taxation last year. At that time, Mr. Speaker, we of the official oposition warned the Minister of Finance that his increases were quite unnecessary to meet the additional costs of our rearmament. In business a surplus is regarded as something of an accomplishment, because it is usually the result of prudent management. But it is not so in government. The surplus in this case is the result of the government having taken more out of the pockets of the people than they needed to meet the legitimate expenses of government. I recall, sir, a statement made by one of the great chancellors of the exchequer, a man who was known as the iron chancellor, Philip Snowden. In one memorable speech he said that any government that takes so much as a sixpence from the people more than it has budgeted to take from them is taking money under false pretences. What will you say then, sir, of a government that has already, in nine months, taken twenty-three times more from the pockets of the people than they budgeted for by way of surplus?
Then we have the hon. member for Coast-Capilano making a speech here two days ago with great enthusiasm. He praised the virtues of this adventitious surplus and decried the efforts of everyone on this side of the house to bring a little realism into the fiscal policies of this government. All the way through he talked about "we"; "we" did this and "we" did that. It was rather strange to hear such talk from him. I was not clear whether he was using the royal or the editorial "we". I am not forgetful of the fact that the hon. member has been in favour in government circles for only the last couple of years. Those of us who were in the last house will remember the same hon. member was made to pay the price for showing a little independence in his expression of views back about 1942. If ever a member was snubbed by the government, it was the member for Coast-Capilano. He was living proof to the Liberal supporters of this government that they had better keep in line. But now, somehow or 
other, since he has been taken back into the fold, he feels he must display all the zeal of the convert.
He made some extraordinary statements which you will find on page 269 of Hansard, and I take a moment to deal with those. He said:
However, when R. B. Bennett was minister of finance he was always out too.
You see he was admitting that his own minister was out in his calculations.
In 1931 he was out not eight per cent but seventeen per cent in his estimate of revenue; and not up, but down. The next year he was exactly the same; he was seventeen per cent down, and had a big deficit.
Mr. Speaker, the facts are very different. In 1931 the government of the day, which had come into office in the previous late summer, was obliged to carry on with the budget brought in by the Mackenzie King government in the spring of 1930. That was the budget that governed the country in the fiscal year 1930-31. It would interest you no doubt, Mr. Speaker, to know that in that famous May-day budget of Mr. Dunning's there was not a word said about an estimate of revenue. It is a most extraordinary budget speech, and I recommend that hon. gentlemen go back and read it. The minister went through his whole budget speech without ever giving the house or the country an estimate of revenues. You will find that mentioned in a speech made by Mr. Bennett on page 1811 of Hansard for May 6, 1930.
The following year Mr. Bennett did bring in a budget, and it is true that he estimated revenues of $403 million, and the revenue, in a situation that no one could have foreseen at that time with the development of a depression, dropped to $335 million. The difference was $68 million for the year. Today this government runs up an error in their estimates creating a surplus of $68 million in just three weeks. Yet, here is the member for Coast-Capilano, a member who supports a government that is running up a budget surplus of $80 million a month, complaining that Mr. Bennett, in the face of an unprecedented situation, was out $68 million in a whole year! It is true that in the following year, when Mr. Rhodes, not Mr. Bennett, was minister of finance, and in the face of a situation that this country shared with all the countries in the world, there was a disappointment of $62 million in estimating the revenues. This amounts to less than the miscalculations of this government amount to in three weeks, and in the face of the plainest of warnings. Enough, however, of this expedition of the parliamentary assistant into the realm of fancy!

I am obliged to bring my remarks to a quick conclusion. This policy of high taxation has deliberately created high prices. Look at what is happening today in our indirect taxes. Prices are so much higher on many commodities than in the United States simply because of our heavy load of indirect taxation, which the United States wisely does not attempt to emulate.
We have smuggling going on at the border as a result, as well.
As the result of increases in direct taxes, here we have the Bell Telephone Company of Canada applying for and obtaining vast increases in rates. Why? Principally because the Minister of Finance has heaped up the taxes upon them. We are facing the same thing in the city of Toronto; we are facing a proposed increase in the rates of the Consumers' Gas Company. The country is faced with increased railway freight rates. Why? Because this government insists upon heaping up the burden of taxation, direct and indirect. We warned them last year these consequences would follow.
I say that the time has come-and this is my final word, Mr. Speaker-when this government should be told to let the people handle their own money. We want to develop the resources of this country. We have to have capital. That capital must come from the savings of the people and from profits. We must have that kind of capital. We must have savings. We cannot have them if the government is going to go on fleecing the people of this country by gouging them with these heavy taxes. We are depending today far too heavily on foreign capital for the development of these resources. We want to see more Canadian capital going into the development of our own Canadian resources. We must have increased savings. We must have increased earnings in Canada. We cannot have those as long as the weight of federal taxation in this country is so seriously retarding Canadian enterprise.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset I should like to congratulate the mover (Mr. George) and the seconder (Mr. Gauthier, Lake St. John) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. At the opening of parliament I feel that our member from New Brunswick did a fine job, and that the hon. member for Lake St. John is a credit to his constituency for the effort he put forth in the house that day.
In the remarks that I will make this afternoon, in no way do I wish to leave the impression in this house that they are critical of the assistance given to the agricultural
The Address-Mr. A. W. Stuart industry in Canada. As I have stated before in this house, the wealth of any country can come from three sources only, namely from land, from sea and from forests. The living conditions in any country are based upon the prosperity of these primary producers. I endorse the government's action in the consideration and the financial assistance which they have given and are still giving the agricultural industry. My criticism is that other primary producers are denied the same generous treatment.
At this time my remarks will be, to a great extent, in connection with the fishing industry; and at this point I want to say that I believe the hon. member for Digby-Yarmouth (Mr. Kirk) and the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Dickey), in the remarks which they made yesterday, would have the support of all the fishermen in the maritime provinces, and they are to be congratulated on the effort they made.
I shall endeavour to present facts in the time at my disposal and to give credit where credit is due. Of the Department of Public Works I want to say that they have provided wharves and breakwaters to protect the fishing fleets of many of the communities where fishing is carried on extensively. I can assure that department that the fishermen are exceedingly grateful. The Department of Transport have provided buoys, lights, whistles and other aids to navigation for which, again I may say, the fishermen are extremely grateful. Some assistance has been given to encourage the building of cold storage facilities. In a small way this assistance has been of help to certain parts of the maritime provinces. At this point, however, I should like to put on the record some of the assistance which the agricultural industry is receiving and has received for many years. I am doing this in order that I may make comparisons as between the agricultural industry and the fishing industry. The record that I shall quote from for the next few minutes is called "Agricultural Assistance, War and Post-War" published by the Department of Agriculture. It is up to date. The latest changes have been registered in this book. I should now like to place on the record a list or table of the different subsidies and the different ways in which assistance is given to the agricultural industry; and I am reading from the table of contents of this publication.
Feeds; freight assistance policy; feed assistance; coarse grains; drawback payments; processing feeds; sugar beet pulp.
Fertilizer and lime.
Dairy products: Fluid and concentrated milk, butter and cheese; cheese export; cheese premium and factory subsidy.

The Address-Mr. A. W. Stuart
Livestock and livestock products: hog premiums; hog freight assistance; hog breeding; bacon export; freight assistance on feeder cattle and lambs; sheep raising, wool, egg export.
Fruits and vegetables: apples; berries for jam; vegetable canning crops; potatoes, potato storage warehouse construction; white and yellow-eye dried beans; white beans; dehydration.
Seeds.
Compensation to farmers for cultivation of milkweed.
Rebate on flax scutching machinery.
The wheat acreage reduction program.
The prairie farm income payments scheme.
The Prairie Farm Assistance Act.
In addition to this, I just want to mention these items, and I want it distinctly understood before I make any mention of them that I am not criticizing in any way the assistance that was given with respect to the several items that I will mention. In addition to what I have already mentioned, there is a 'payment of $65 million that was made by the Department of Agriculture in 1951-just last year-to the Canadian wheat board to be distributed to the wheat growers of western Canada. There was the Fraser valley flood where $14 million of the money of the Canadian people were spent. Again I have no criticism to offer. Then there was the P.ed river flood. I have not the figure for that but I believe it was somewhere in the neighbourhood of the same amount. There were several disastrous fires in connection with which the people affected received benefits from the federal government. I endorse that action in every way in the world. With respect to the wheat that they were unable to harvest in western Canada last fall, the farmers have received assistance. That assistance has my wholehearted support. Just a few days ago in this house legislation was passed to provide assistance for those who had been affected by the foot-and-mouth disease which has broken out in western Canada. Again I support the government's attitude in that respect in every way.
At this point I might mention that in our fishing industry we have had maladies which were perhaps just as serious to that industry as is this foot-and-mouth disease to the cattle producers of this country; but no financial assistance was given to the fishing industry. We had an outbreak among the sardines in the early thirties, and it was an exceedingly serious thing. Thousands of tons of sardines were condemned by the inspectors at the canneries, for which the fishermen would get perhaps one-tenth of a cent a pound as fertilizer. We went through that period. The outbreak cleared up for a while but it returned again, and we have had it off and on for the last twenty years. But all during that period not a single dollar was paid out of the consolidated fund of this country in
[Hr. Stuart (Charlotte).]
order to assist any of those fishermen. The matter has been brought to the attention of the government on many occasions, but I suppose that perhaps it has not been brought to their attention forcibly enough.
In the last ten years $20 million has been spent to assist the apple growers in the Annapolis valley. I am going to have very little to say on this score, because perhaps my remarks would not meet with the approval of quite a few hon. members, but I just want that amount to go on record. Over $20 million is an enormous amount of money to be used to assist one small branch of the agricultural industry.
During the discussion in this chamber on the foot-and-mouth disease suggestions came from hon. members sitting here that, if carried out, would have made money available even to working men in packing houses. They would have received some sort of compensation because of the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease in western Canada. If that discussion had continued for a few more days they would have reverted back and back until indirectly thousands and thousands of people would have been involved. Why men working in packing houses should be considered for compensation in a case of this kind when they have unemployment insurance is something that I fail to understand. If these people were out of work and without any means of supporting themselves I again would be prepared to endorse it. But I believe that the legislation we already have on the statute books and already in force will take care of the situation.
I now want to turn to page 2 of this report, from which I read a few minutes ago, to cite a few items that come under the support of the Department of Agriculture. Subsidies were paid on agricultural machinery, binder twine, rope, bags and bagging, feed, fertilizer, harness and saddlery, lumber, pesticides, petroleum and woodenware, and bees. When I look at that list and I see included binder twine and rope subsidized for the agricultural industry of this country, I look back to my own county down in the maritime provinces and realize that netting that we were buying in 1945 for 70 cents a pound is costing today $2.40 a pound. There has never been any suggestion of a subsidy to fishermen to buy twine. Where ten pounds of twine are used in western Canada for the purpose that it may be used, thousands of pounds are used in the Ashing industry all along that coast line.
Then we come to rope. The hon. member for Digby-Yarmouth yesterday put on the record the cost of building lobster traps, and included in that cost was rope, which is very

The Address-Mr. A. W. Stuart
necessary. Thousands and thousands of pounds of rope are used every year in that industry. Today we are paying nearly four times the price that we paid for it in 1945. There has never been any suggestion that there should be any subsidy payment of any kind to these fishermen.
There is one other small item in the list, pesticides, which brings me to coal tar. Coal tar is a product which is used extensively in the fishing industry. I think that item of "pesticides" or "insecticides" may be used for the same purpose as coal tar in many cases. Coal tar is used to protect netting, and in some parts of the maritime provinces it is necessary for them to dip their entire lobster pots in the coal tar to save them from the marine borers. In 1946 we were paying $4.50 a barrel, and I believe it did get up to $5 in the latter part of the year. It is a tar that is very thin and it is utterly impossible to use it for any other purpose. Today that tar is $22 a barrel and the fishermen are still paying the sales tax. I brought this matter to the attention of the Department of National Revenue. They are still paying over $2 a barrel tax on coal tar. Again if that had a subsidy payment, or even if that tax were removed completely, it would be a great assistance to the fishing industry.
Another item that is mentioned here is petroleum. I am not sure just what petroleum means, or what it would cover in this item to the benefit of the farmers, but I can assure you that in the fishing industry a great deal of petroleum is used. So far as this government is concerned there has never been any thought of assistance to the fishermen in that regard. Another item that is mentioned is lumber. Just what that word covers, or what territory it takes in, again it is impossible to explain; but lumber is used in all branches of the fishing industry. A subsidy or any assistance given to the fishing industry would be greatly appreciated.
On page 3 of the same report there is this brief statement;
To make more short-and-intermediate term credit available, the dominion government in 1944 passed the Farm Improvements Loan Act. Chartered banks are guaranteed against loss up to 10 per cent of the amount loaned by them under the act (a maximum of $250 million).
In maritime language that is a lot of money. Further down the page appears this brief statement:
New activities in the postwar period include a commitment on the part of the dominion government to support farm prices. The Agricultural Prices Support Act of 1944 states:
"In prescribing prices the board shall endeavour to ensure adequate and stable returns for agriculture by promoting orderly adjustment from war
to peace conditions and shall endeavour to secure a fair relationship between the returns from agriculture and those from other occupations."
Those would be very kind words indeed for the men engaged in the fishing industry. They would be glad to realize that that would apply to them. It would give them a great feeling of security if they knew that the paragraph that I have just read also applied to the industry in which they are engaged.
I want to go back for a few minutes to an item that I found. I was just searching at random for a few items for comparison. I found one on page 6 of the estimates for 1951-52, namely, item 43, which reads;
To provide assistance for the replacement of maple production equipment.
When I saw that item I realized immediately that the maple products of this country would be a very small item in comparison with the fishing industry. When I looked at the item I found that for some few years we have had an annual grant of $500,000 given to that industry. I immediately tried to find out just what this $500,000 was voted for. I was informed yesterday that a few years ago it was discovered that maple syrup was of a much better quality if all the containers used in its manufacture were of aluminum. Since that time the federal government has voted $500,000 annually to buy aluminum pails for the maple syrup industry of this country. I am using this as a comparison. When you compare that industry, which operates about two weeks out of fifty-two, with the fishing industry you find that during that same period in 1951 $240,000 was paid out by the fisheries support board. Many hon. members may have the feeling that the Fisheries Prices Support Act applies the same as the Agricultural Prices Support Act. I want to assure them and the people of this country that there is no comparison whatever. In the year 1951, $240,000 was paid out under that act, and each and every dollar was paid to the salt codfish industry in Newfoundland. Not a single dollar came to any one of the other provinces, and that amount is only 50 per cent of the amount that was paid to the maple syrup producers of the Dominion of Canada. When I look back and I see a record, such as this-and this is one that I picked at random-I begin to wonder. Then I looked a little further down. I see my friend, the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruick-shank), sitting over there.

Fruit, vegetables and maple products, and honey, Including grant of $5,000 to the Canadian Horticultural Council.
I find that the greatest part of that vote was to buy boxes, barrels and other containers for the berry producers of British Columbia. And I am not quarrelling with that.

Just a moment, now;
I am not quarrelling with that. But down in the maritime provinces we have been buying boxes for a long time. Down in the maritimes the people engaged in the fishing industry
[Mr. Stuart (Charlotte) .1

need pails, hogsheads, tanks and other containers; but I have yet to hear any suggestion that there should be any subsidy paid in that connection.
I am not quarrelling with the people out there, if they need these things-but in that connection I find in the same book from which I read earlier a statement by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) which might be of interest:
In other words, the government has become responsible for the financing of the berries. We have an undertaking, both from the producers and the provincial government, which has been much concerned with the matter, that acreages will be cut down this year to a point where they will more nearly approach the possible market. I may say that the acreages have been cut down somewhat by the floods and they are undertaking to cut them even more.
And the last paragraph:
It is not a floor price that is being put under berries. As a matter of fact, the greater part of it is to pay for the containers the cost of which we guarantee.
That is a statement from the records of the Department of Agriculture, and I believe it is correct. Again I should like to say in passing that I fail to understand why every branch of agriculture requires this assistance, and why at the same time the fishing industry is completely ignored. This has been brought to the attention of the house by members from Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick, Newfoundland, Quebec and British Columbia; but it is utterly impossible to make them understand that this industry, this enormous fishing industry we have in Canada, has much to do with the economy of the country. Half these people who go down to the sea in ships produce this food under conditions under which a farmer would turn his back. I am speaking from experience, because I have been on the water both winter and summer. I did not go out on the water for six or eight months, and then take my family south for the winter. I did not go on the water for six or eight months and then sit by the fireside for the remainder of the year. I was on the water twelve months of the year, and I believe I am in a position to understand just what these men have gone through, down through the years.
I do not believe it will be found that they are asking for any special privileges. That is not what they want. I have only two or three moments left before the six o'clock adjournment, and in that time I would point out that during this last year the sardine industry of the islands of Grand Manan, Campobello and Deer island was nearly a complete failure. Those fishermen took what remained of their lifetime earnings last winter,

and they purchased materials, the wood and twine necessary to build sardine weirs. Many ol them borrowed money. Last spring they built the weirs once again, but the industry was a complete failure.
This winter has been a very windy and tough one along the coast line. Those structures need repairing. But, again, because of the complete failure of the industry last year, the fishermen have not the cash to put back into it this year, and their credit is exhausted. It is a pretty bleak outlook.
This matter has been brought to the attention of the Department of Fisheries, and I hope that some way may be found to give assistance. This cannot continue indefinitely, a condition where one primary producer is singled out for special consideration, while at the same time another primary producer is
12,	1952
The Address-Mr. A. W. Stuart completely ignored. That set-up will not work in a democratic country. We must try to equalize the assistance given.
Before adjourning the debate may I say that, in looking over the situation, we must face the fact that these primary producers are the backbone of the country. Without them there is nothing. It is what they take out of the soil, out of the sea and out of the forests that brings about the prosperity enjoyed here.
On motion of Mr. Stuart (Charlotte) the debate was adjourned.
